sections.title: Vinaceous-brown cap
sections.text: Inocybe tricolor Kühner is a small fibrecap. In Kuyper’s revision, the cap reaches 38 mm, flattens while retaining a broad, blunt umbo, and is dark vinaceous brown, paler toward the margin. Its surface is fibrillose to finely squamulose; the margin may become slightly rimulose with age.

sections.title: Gills and reddish stem
sections.text: The gills are very crowded, greyish yellow and adnate, with a white-flocculose edge that may turn vinaceous when damaged. The described stem is about 50 × 5 mm, fairly equal and solid, whitish at the apex then orange-red to vinaceous lower down; it is slightly pruinose at the very top and fibrillose farther down. The flesh is whitish in the cap and orange-red to vinaceous in the stem.

sections.title: Smell and microscopic characters
sections.text: Kuyper’s description notes a smell reminiscent of Peru balsam. The spores are smooth, regular to slightly amygdaloid, with a somewhat conical apex; those measured for the described collection were 7.0–9.0 × 5.0–6.0 µm. Microscopy and examined specimens are needed to support an identification: this illustration cannot identify a foraged mushroom.

sections.title: Ecology, rarity and caution
sections.text: In central Europe the species is reported under Norway spruce (Picea abies) on calcareous soil. Norway’s red-list account also records calcareous spruce or pine forests and Dryas heath, while noting that the mycorrhizal hosts there are only presumed; it assesses the species as Near Threatened (NT) in Norway. One specimen identified as I. tricolor tested positive for psilocybin, while muscarine was not detected in the 1985 analysis. This single result does not characterize every population and does not establish safety; edibility remains unassessed.

traits: Cap up to about 38 mm, dark vinaceous brown and paler at the margin, fibrillose to finely squamulose, with a broad blunt umbo
Very crowded, greyish-yellow, adnate gills with a whitish edge that may stain vinaceous
Solid, fairly equal stem, whitish at the top then orange-red to vinaceous lower down
Flesh whitish in the cap and orange-red to vinaceous in the stem
Smooth, regular to slightly amygdaloid spores, about 7–9 × 5–6 µm in the description consulted
Reported under Picea abies on calcareous soil in central Europe; Norwegian mycorrhizal ecology remains partly hypothetical
safetyNote: Psilocybin was detected in one specimen identified as I. tricolor; an older analysis of one specimen cannot establish the composition of every collection or assess a dose or risk. This rare species requires specialist identification; do not consume based on this entry or image.
